title: Live from San Francisco: How Malls Work
summary: Live recording at the Castro Theater in San Francisco (Sunday afternoon, during San Francisco Sketch Fest) about the history of the shopping mall. The hosts trace shopping districts from ancient Rome's Trajan's Market and the Grand Bazaar in Istanbul, through department stores and early enclosed arcades like Providence's Westminster Arcade, to Victor Gruen's Southdale Center in Edina, Minnesota (1956), which introduced the enclosed, air-conditioned, two-level mall with anchor department stores. They cover the mall's golden age from 1956 to 2000s, mall nostalgia (Cinnabon, Orange Julius, Spencer Gifts, Chess King), mall movies, mall walkers, the West Edmonton Mall and Mall of America, Gruen's disavowal of the mall and his anti-car views, the Gruen transfer, mall music and atmosphere design, and the mall's decline after 2007 due to the Great Recession, online retail, and tax depreciation rules that encouraged building and then selling malls. They close with the Randall Park Mall in North Randall, Ohio, and the rise of lifestyle centers and outdoor high-end malls.

segments.title: Opening banter at the Castro Theater
segments.summary: Hosts open the live show in San Francisco at the Castro Theater, joke about the episode topic, and preview the history of the mall.

segments.title: Ancient markets and early shopping districts
segments.summary: Trajan's Market in ancient Rome (built around 107) is described as the world's oldest shopping center, and the Grand Bazaar in Istanbul (built 1455-1461) as an early long-running market. Medieval market towns and the importance of centralized commerce are discussed.

segments.title: Department stores and early enclosed arcades
segments.summary: Department stores such as Marshall Field and Company in Chicago and J. L. Hudson's in Detroit are discussed. The Westminster Arcade in Providence, Rhode Island is described as an early enclosed shopping center, and the Ghostvedes Voor (Dutch-style covered arcade) is mentioned.

segments.title: Northland Center and Victor Gruen's design
segments.summary: Northland Center in Southfield, Michigan, an open-air center with an anchor Hudson's store, is described. Victor Gruen, the Austrian-born architect, is introduced as the designer behind the modern mall, and the idea of placing two department stores with smaller shops between them is explained.

segments.title: Southdale Center opens in Edina, 1956
segments.summary: Southdale in Edina, Minnesota, opened in 1956 as the first fully enclosed, climate-controlled, two-level mall, commissioned by Dayton's. Its design features an introverted layout, skylights, gardens, and multi-level parking. The grand opening drew about 75,000 people and national press coverage.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break and a brief return from the break with a note about the printed script.

segments.title: Golden age of the mall and mall nostalgia
segments.summary: Between 1956 and 2000 roughly thousands of malls were built in the US. Lisa Sharon Davis's book is cited on the mall's cultural role. The hosts discuss family mall days and mall-born brands such as Cinnabon, Orange Julius, Chick-fil-A and Spencer Gifts, and their personal mall memories.

segments.title: Mall movies and giant malls
segments.summary: Malls in film are discussed, including Fast Times at Ridgemont High (Sherman Oaks Galleria), Commando, the Blues Brothers, and Back to the Future (Puente Hills Mall stand-in). The Valley Girl song by Moon Unit Zappa is mentioned. The West Edmonton Mall and Mall of America are described for their size and attractions.

segments.title: Mall walkers and Douglas Coupland
segments.summary: Mall walkers, mostly older adults who walk malls before opening, are described, including Mall of America's program and a CDC report on mall walking. Douglas Coupland's remarks at the Mall of America opening are recounted.

segments.title: Mall psychology: Gruen transfer, music, and the Supreme Court
segments.summary: The Gruen transfer effect is defined. Malcolm Gladwell's concept of threshold resistance is cited. Mall music and facilities management are discussed. Gruen's disappointment with the mall is covered, including the 1976 Hudgens v. NLRB Supreme Court decision that barred picketing inside a private mall, and his disavowal of paternity of the mall in 1978.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break before the segment on the mall's decline.

segments.title: Decline of the mall
segments.summary: Mall construction peaked in 1990 and stopped around 2007. The Great Recession, shift to Walmart and Target, dependence on struggling anchor stores, and online retail (about half of traditional retailer sales from the web by 2014) are presented as causes of decline.

segments.title: Tax depreciation loophole and Randall Park Mall
segments.summary: The accelerated depreciation tax rule of the 1950s-60s is explained as the driver of mall overbuilding and flipping. Randall Park Mall in North Randall, Ohio, which opened with a large celebration and later closed, is described. Lifestyle centers and outdoor high-end malls such as Rick Caruso's projects are discussed as the mall's next form.

segments.title: Closing thoughts and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts reflect on the mall as a consumer church and civic space, then sign off with a plug for the show's website.
